doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Gospel church band, first saxophone and a strict household
summary: Murray got his alto at nine from Phil Hardymon, played in the family church band, and chafed at the ban on jazz at home until his mother died when he was 13.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah. Certainly. When I was younger I started out in Gospel music. I remember the day I got my saxophone of Phil Hardymon, he came into the system, at the Berkeley, California school system. He is the one that handed me my alto. And he passed away a few years ago. A great trumpet player, Phil Hardymon. He is the one who is really responsible for bringing jazz into the Berkeley school system. And so that night I played the saxophone at church. I’m sure I was squeaking and sounding very strange, very much like I sound now but I had no idea what I was doing. My mother was playing piano, my brother on clarinet, my cousin playing trumpet, my father was playing guitar. I knew the songs but I didn’t know the fingerings, but I was working on it. A few weeks later I blended right in. I had been playing bongos with them for like a couple of years already, but at nine, that was where I was. And I had taken piano lessons for two years already with a stride piano player that my mother put me with. And with me it was always, wherever I was, I felt comfortable there, but I also yearned to play other things. Like I strived to get out of church music in fact. Because we were the church band, we played every night, well three nights a week at least and all day Sunday. And after a while, you know, I’m a young man, I’m a teenager, I wanted to get out, I wanted to play gigs, I wanted to do different, I wanted to play blues gigs, so I’m starting to go out and do these kinds of things. I grew up in a very strict Church of God and Christ environment, where playing or practicing jazz in our house was forbidden. So I had to go out to my friends’ places to practice and play that kind of music. After my mother passed away, when I was 13, things became a little looser because all of sudden this was three boys and a father, © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

and no mother. And he couldn’t watch us all the time so I started bringing my things in the house and next thing I know my father got a little looser in terms of the Devil’s music and what I could play at home. And I started playing, I even had the guys over for rehearsal. So that’s how loose it became after my mother had passed away. So I always yearned to play other styles. So I’m playing R&B now, and also, I’m coming from Berkeley, California so in order to play gigs you have to know a large repertoire, also rock & roll. You have to know how to appease the people on the Berkeley campus, we’re playing for a lot of parties and different things at UC Berkeley, things like that. So we played all of the rock material. The Grateful Dead was there, we played that stuff.
